title.en: Temiya the Mute Prince (Mugapakkha Jataka, no. 538)
title.zh: 啞子特彌雅本生（第五百三十八）

texts.period: Jataka no. 538, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by E. B. Cowell, 1907

region.en: Benares and the Himalaya hermitage (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈與雪山精舍（象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 6 (trans. E. B. Cowell, 1907)

summary.en: A queen's Act of Truth wins a heaven-sent son, Temiya; at one month old he hears his father doom four robbers, recalls twenty years as king and eighty thousand years in the Ussada hell, and resolves to escape kingship by feigning lame, deaf and dumb. Sixteen years of tests fail; condemned to be buried alive, he stirs at the chariot-threshold, reveals superhuman strength, and becomes an ascetic who draws his parents, court and city after him.
summary.zh: 王后以諦誓感天，帝釋送下天神之子特彌雅；滿月時聞父判處四盜極刑，憶起前生為王二十年、墮等活地獄八萬年，決意假裝跛聾啞以逃王位。歷經十六年種種試探皆不失分毫；被判活埋之日，車輪觸門檻而他動念，現超凡臂力，出家為仙人，父母、宮廷、舉城相隨。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Queen Candadevi of Benares, childless while sixteen thousand wives were barren, lay keeping the Uposatha vows and protested: if I have never broken the commandments, may a son be borne to me. Sakka's dwelling grew hot, and he found the Bodhisatta - who in a former birth had reigned twenty years in Benares and then suffered eighty thousand years in the Ussada hell - waiting to rise from the world of the gods. Come to the world of men, he told him, you will fully exercise the perfections. Born wet on a day of rain, the prince was named Temiya; and at a month old, lying on his father's knee, he heard the king doom four robbers to the thorn-whip, chains, the spear and the stake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mugapakkha Jataka (no. 538) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: At that his memory of former births returned: I was a king for twenty years, and I burned in the Ussada hell for eighty thousand; if I become a king I shall be born again in hell. A goddess in the white umbrella - his mother in a birth long past - counseled him: show no intelligence; be a fool in all men's eyes. For sixteen years the court tried him with sixteen great tests: they withheld his milk and set out cakes and fruit, which the other children seized, while he sat unmoved; they built a blazing palm-leaf house around him; they loosed a trained elephant and serpents with hoods spread over his head; they burst conches behind a curtain, blazed lamps in the dark, smeared him with molasses for the flies, let pans of fire under his bed, and filled his chamber with celestial dancing-girls - and not a hand or foot stirred, not a tear fell, though his mother's heart was well-nigh rent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mugapakkha Jataka (no. 538) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fortune-tellers confessed an ill omen had been hidden, and the king resolved to bury his crippled, deaf, dumb son alive. Candadevi spent her unclaimed boon on seven days of kingship for the boy, and spent the nights imploring him to speak; but he lay still till the last morning, when Sunanda the charioteer lifted him like a bundle of flowers into the chariot. At the eastern gate the wheel struck the threshold - my desire has attained its end, thought Temiya. At the wood he rubbed his limbs and rose: the earth rose to meet his foot, and he lifted the chariot's hinder end like a child's toy-cart. Adorned by Sakka's craftsman, he told the awed charioteer why he had played the cripple, took the hermit's dress in a hermitage three leagues wide, and when the king and queen came out to fetch him home, taught them and all the city until king, queens, courtiers, citizens - and an invading king who arrived the same day - took the ascetic vow. The charioteer was Sariputta, and the wise Mugapakkha was myself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mugapakkha Jataka (no. 538) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

title.en: Mahajanaka Swims the Ocean (Mahajanaka Jataka, no. 539)
title.zh: 大那迦海渡本生（第五百三十九）

texts.period: Jataka no. 539, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by E. B. Cowell, 1907

region.en: Mithila, kingdom of Videha, India; the open ocean as symbolic passage (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 彌提羅（韋提呵國）；大海為象徵通道（象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 6 (trans. E. B. Cowell, 1907)

summary.en: Orphaned by his uncle's usurpation, Mahajanaka sails for trade; the ship founders and for seven days he swims the open sea, arguing with the goddess Manimekhala that a man must strive to the last - until she carries him to Mithila, where the festal chariot finds him asleep on a ceremonial stone and crowns him. Later the mango-tree lesson - fruitful trees are broken, barren ones stand - turns him to renunciation, and neither burning city nor weeping wife can hold him.
summary.zh: 叔父篡位、父王戰死，大那迦王子出海經商；船隻沉沒，他於大海中奮力泅游七日，與海女神辯論「縱死於努力，亦免於咎」；女神感其志，抱之飛至彌提羅，慶典車輦尋得沉睡於石上的王子而灌頂立為王。後因見芒果樹「有果者枝折，無果者青翠」而悟世間之患，決意出家；火燒城、斷路線、泣別之妻皆不能挽留。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: King Aritthajanaka of Mithila imprisoned his brother Polajanaka on a slave's slander, but the prisoner's solemn protest burst his chains and the door; raising a host on the frontier he gave the king battle or the umbrella, and the king fell. His queen fled by night with a basket of jewels on her head, carrying the Bodhisatta in her womb; Sakka, feeling the world shake with the child's majesty, drove her thirty leagues to Campa in a covered carriage as an old man, and a brahmin teacher sheltered her as a sister. The boy she bore was named Mahajanaka; teased as the widow's son, he bit his mother's breast till she told him whose son he was.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mahajanaka Jataka (no. 539) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Refusing his mother's jewels for war, he took half and sailed for Suvannabhumi to win wealth first. In seven days the ship had run seven hundred leagues, then strained apart and sank; the crew wept and called on their gods, but Mahajanaka neither wept nor prayed: he filled himself with sugar and ghee, oiled his two garments, and stood leaning on the mast as the sea turned red with the drowned. He struck out for Mithila and swam seven days; then the sea-guardian Manimekhala, seven days remiss, stood before him in the air - who art thou, striving here, far from land? Knowing my duty in the world, to strive while I can, he answered; and though she told him the shoreless deep must kill him, he said: he who does all a man can do is free from blame - and she carried him as her child through the air to Mithila and laid him on the ceremonial stone in a mango grove.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mahajanaka Jataka (no. 539) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dead Polajanaka had left his kingdom to whoever could please his daughter Sivali, tell the head of the square bed, string a bow of a thousand men's strength, and draw out sixteen hidden treasures. The festal chariot halted before the sleeping prince; he turned on his side, unhurried, and was anointed king on the spot. He answered Sivali's tests - the golden needle, the thousand-man bow, the sixteen treasures - and ruled all Videha. Years later a mango tree stripped bare by fruit-seekers taught him that the fruitful are broken while the barren stand; he renounced the throne, and though Sivali loosed seven hundred wives upon him and kindled false fires in Mithila, and he drew a line none might cross, only the playing girl with one silent bracelet - wouldst thou be happy? be alone - and the fletcher with one eye shut could show him the way: he went north, and Sivali raised topes where he had talked and herself became an ascetic destined for the Brahma world. Narada was the ascetic, the sea-goddess Uppalavanna, Sivali Rahula's mother, and I myself was King Mahajanaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mahajanaka Jataka (no. 539) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

title.en: Sama the Archer's Son (Sama Jataka, no. 540)
title.zh: 睒摩孝子本生（第五百四十）

texts.period: Jataka no. 540, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by E. B. Cowell, 1907

region.en: Himalaya, hermitage on the river Migasammata (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山彌伽沙摩陀河畔精舍（象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 6 (trans. E. B. Cowell, 1907)

summary.en: Two hermits born of hunter families conceive the golden child Sama by Sakka's counsel; a snake's poisonous breath blinds both parents, and Sama alone tends them. The venal king Piliyakkha, hunting for venison, shoots him at the water's edge; dying, Sama entrusts his parents to his own killer - and by the goddess's pity and the parents' and goddess's Acts of Truth the poison loses its force, Sama springs up whole, his parents' sight returns, and the king gives up his bow.
summary.zh: 獵戶出身的二位仙人依帝釋之請，以觸臍之法感得金身之子睒摩；一蛇毒氣致二老雙目失明，睒摩獨力奉養。波羅奈王畢利耶叉貪鹿肉而來狩獵，於取水處誤射睒摩；睒摩垂死仍託孤於射他之人——賴宿世之母的天人憐憫，與父母、天人三者諦誓之力，毒散而睒摩躍起如常，父母雙目復明，國王棄弓行施。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: A rich merchant's son of Savatthi was ordained only after winning his parents' leave, and when his folk fell to beggary while he strove twelve years for insight without reaching it, he resolved to give back the yellow robe and keep them. The Master praised him - well done, well done: in old time, going my alms-round, I supported my parents - and told this tale. Dukula and Parika, children of two hunter chiefs wed as their fathers had promised, were pure beings newly come from the Brahma world; though born of hunters they killed nothing, and with their parents' leave became hermits on the river Migasammata in a hut Sakka caused to be built, where beasts felt only kindness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sama Jataka (no. 540) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Foreseeing they would lose their sight, Sakka counseled Dukula at the due season to touch Parika's navel with his hand; and the Bodhisatta, descending from the heaven of the Thirty-three, was conceived and born golden-hued - Suvannasama, whom the kinnari nymphs adorned in their caves. In age past the parents had been a physician and his wife, who blinded an ungrateful patient's eye; and now, sheltering from a storm on an anthill, they were struck blind by the snake that lived there. Sama led them home by a long pole, stretched ropes through the hermitage to mark every path, and from that day fetched water, swept, cooked, and gathered fruit with a troop of deer while they kept within.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sama Jataka (no. 540) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: King Piliyakkha of Benares, drunk with desire for venison, had left his kingdom to his mother and gone up into the Himalaya killing deer; he ambushed by the water where Sama came down with his jar between two led deer, and loosed a poisoned arrow through his right side. Who, as I filled my water-jar, has wounded me from ambush? asked the dying man, and would not accuse: the king lied of a fleeing deer, then confessed. Learning that blind parents waited on the boy's care, the king wept that one shaft had slain the three - and vowed to serve them as Sama had done. The goddess Bahusodari, his mother seven births before, saw all; the parents and the goddess made their solemn asseverations - that he lived virtuously, spoke truth and nursed his parents; that the poison lose its force - and Sama sprang up young, fair and vigorous, while his parents' sight returned in the same moment. The king took the ten duties of a king from his lips, gave great gifts and went to heaven; Sama and his parents passed to the Brahma world. The king was Ananda, and Suvannasama was I myself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sama Jataka (no. 540) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

title.en: King Nimi's Tour of Hell and Heaven (Nimi Jataka, no. 541)
title.zh: 尼彌王遊地獄天宮本生（第五百四十一）

texts.period: Jataka no. 541, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by E. B. Cowell, 1907

region.en: Mithila, kingdom of Videha; hell and heaven realms as symbolic vision (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 彌提羅（韋提呵國）；地獄與天界為象徵所見（象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 6 (trans. E. B. Cowell, 1907)

summary.en: Nimi, last of a line of eighty-four thousand kings who each renounced at the first grey hair, wonders whether holy life or alms bears more fruit; Sakka sends the charioteer Matali, who first drives him through hell - the burning river Vetarani, vultures on misers, red-hot lumps, the pit of coals, the iron cauldron - then up through the heavens, where each jeweled mansion tells the merit of the good man within. Offered immortal pleasures, Nimi declines what another's hand bestows, returns, and in his turn renounces the world.
summary.zh: 尼彌王乃八萬四千位「見白髮即出家」的君王之末裔。他自問：持戒與布施何者功德更大？帝釋遣馭者摩多利駕天車相迎，先引他下觀地獄：誾摩尼彼岸沸火之河、啄食慳吝者的禿鷲、烙紅的石塊、炭火坑、鐵鑊，並一一指明各種罪業；再引他上天，一一示現由善行所感的天宮。帝釋願授不死之樂，尼彌王卻拒受他人之手所賜之福，歸國後循先祖之例於芒果園出家。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: In the mango park of Mithila the Master smiled, remembering how he had meditated there in the time of King Makhadeva. Four and eighty thousand years Makhadeva took his pleasure as a young man, was viceroy as long, and reigned as long; then, at the first grey hair his barber showed him - God's messengers, he called them - he set his son on the throne and became a hermit, and so did son after son, four and eighty thousand princes less two. The first of the line, watching from Brahma's heaven, resolved to round off the family himself, and was reborn as Nimi, Prince Hoop. Nimi built five alms-halls and gave five hundred thousand a day, kept the fasts, preached the Law, and heaven filled and hell stood as it were empty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Nimi Jataka (no. 541) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: As he gave, a doubt arose: which is more fruitful - holy life or giving alms? Sakka's throne grew hot, and he came down blazing to answer: not by any charity are those states won that hermits win by austerity. The gods of the Thirty-three, hearing of their teacher, begged to see him; Sakka sent the charioteer Matali, and at the full moon a second moon rose over Mithila - no, the people cried, it is a chariot! Matali asked which road he would see first, the home of the righteous or of the wicked. Let me see the place of sinful men, said Nimi, for go to heaven I must in any case - and Matali showed him the river Vetarani, hot, stinking, covered with burning flame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Nimi Jataka (no. 541) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Question by question Matali taught how sin ripens: the creatures devoured by black dogs and speckled vultures were churls foul-tongued to brahmins and ascetics; those pounded with red-hot lumps had tormented the innocent; those struggling in the pit of coals had suborned witnesses and forsworn debts before a crowd; the great iron cauldron boiled the rest. Then he drove upward, and mansion after mansion of crystal, jewels and gold rose in the air, each the fruit of a generous householder who gave parks and wells, fed the tranquil saints and kept the sabbath. Past Cittakuta's gateway, ringed with Indra's statues, they came to Sudhamma hall, where the Thirty-three welcomed their teacher and Sakka offered him immortal pleasures. I care not for blessings given by another's hand, Nimi answered; my goods are mine when on my deeds I stand - I will go and do much good among men. After seven days he returned, exhorted the people to almsgiving, and when his barber found the first white hair he gave him a village, set his son on the throne and took the hermit's path in the same mango park. Anuruddha was Sakka, Ananda was Matali, and King Nimi was I myself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Nimi Jataka (no. 541) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

title.en: The Serpent Prince in the Snake-Charmer's Basket (Bhuridatta Jataka, no. 543)
title.zh: 龍王子被縛本生（第五百四十三）

texts.period: Jataka no. 543, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by E. B. Cowell, 1907

region.en: Yamuna river bank and the Naga underworld beneath it (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 閻浮那河畔及其地下龍宮世界（象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 6 (trans. E. B. Cowell, 1907)

summary.en: The Naga prince Bhuridatta, son of a Benares princess and the serpent king Dhatarattha, keeps fast-day vows on an anthill by the Yamuna, bidding the world take his skin or his blood; a hunter-brahmin he once enriched sells him to the snake-charmer Alambayana, who crushes him with drugs and spells and tours him dancing for a month - until his mother's dream, his brother's wager with a frog-poisoned princess and the king's terror free him, the charmer is stricken leprous, and the traitor is forgiven before the Naga court.
summary.zh: 龍王子波利達多（母為波羅奈公主、父為龍王婆藪達多）於閻浮那河畔蟻封持守齋戒，任人取其皮血；昔受其恩惠的獵戶婆羅門將他賣給弄蛇師阿蘭婆衍那，術士以藥咒折其齒、碎其骨，令其獻技一月逐村斂財——賴其母噩夢、兄長之蛙毒公主賭局與國王之懼，龍子得釋；術士染癩，賣主被押至龍庭，波利達多寬恕之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); serpent-underworld imagery belongs to the shared naga corpus and is retold freely; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Exiled by a suspicious father to a hut on the Yamuna, prince Brahmadatta was won by a widowed Naga woman who tested him with flower-beds; their children were Sagara-Brahmadatta and Samuddaja. A tortoise, condemned to the whirlpool by the king's frightened sons, escaped into the Naga world by posing as a marriage envoy, and soon the serpent kings ringed Benares with their coils until the king gave Samuddaja to Dhatarattha, not knowing she was going among snakes; a proclamation forbade any to show snake-nature before her, and she bore four sons, learning the truth only when the infant Arittha showed his serpent form and lost an eye to her terrified nail. The third son was Datta, named Bhuridatta by Sakka himself for the wisdom with which he answered the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bhuridatta Jataka (no. 543) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seeing the glory of Sakka's court, Bhuridatta longed for the world of the gods and asked leave to keep the fast. Within the Naga realm his snake-maidens hindered him, so he went to the haunts of men, folded his body on an anthill by the banyan, and lay with hoods contracted, saying aloud: let who will take my skin, muscles, bones or blood. A hunter-brahmin whom he had once carried to the Naga world and loaded with four hundred Naga maidens, coming by with his son Somadatta, saw the jewel guarded by a thousand Naga youths and sold the secret to the snake-charmer Alambayana for a wish-fulfilling gem - though Somadatta, crying that hell yawns for the traitor, fled to become an ascetic. Alambayana anointed himself, ate his drugs, spat the spell into the serpent's mouth, seized him by the tail and broke him with the cloth-wrap and the rope-rubbing till his body streamed blood; the Bodhisatta, fearing only to break his virtue, neither opened his eyes full nor felt anger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bhuridatta Jataka (no. 543) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Stuffed into a creeper basket, the serpent king danced as he was bidden - great or small, round or heaped, one hood or a hundred, blue, yellow, red or white, emitting water or smoke - and the charmer gleaned a hundred thousand pieces in one village and a king's audience in Benares. In the Naga world his mother saw in a dream a black man lop off her arm, and set out with her sons to search; Sudassana went as an ascetic with the frog-princess Accimukhi hidden in his hair, found his brother at the palace court, and staked five thousand pieces on her: three drops of her poison that no earth, sky or sea could receive were let fall into prepared holes, and the flame that burst out struck Alambayana white with leprosy till he cried thrice, I will set the snake-king free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bhuridatta Jataka (no. 543) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bhuridatta rose radiant from the basket; the king of Benares found these were his own sister's sons; and back in the Naga world the traitor-brahmin, hauled out of his sin-washing by Subhaga, was judged by Dhatarattha - who forgave him, taught him a brahmin's true duties, and let him go to become an ascetic. Bhuridatta kept the precepts all his life and with the host of Nagas went to fill the seats of heaven. The outcast brahmin was Devadatta, Somadatta was Ananda, and I was Bhuridatta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bhuridatta Jataka (no. 543) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

title.en: Great Brahma Narada Answers the King (Mahanaradakassapa Jataka, no. 544)
title.zh: 大梵那羅陀說法本生（第五百四十四）

texts.period: Jataka no. 544, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by E. B. Cowell, 1907

region.en: Mithila, kingdom of Videha, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 彌提羅（韋提呵國，印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 6 (trans. E. B. Cowell, 1907)

summary.en: When King Angati of Videha takes the naked ascetic Guna's doctrine that there is no other world and no fruit of virtue, his daughter Ruja - who remembers seven past and seven future births - pleads all night in parables without success, and prays to the ten directions; Brahma Narada descends in an ascetic's garb, wagers five hundred against a thousand in the next world, paints the hells waiting for the faithless, and turns the king to the five precepts and almsgiving.
summary.zh: 韋提呵國王阿拏耋聽信裸形外道裘那「無來世、無善惡業報」之說；其女魯闍憶七世過去與七世未來（鐵匠之子、山羊、獼猴、閹牛、非男非女、天女……），徹夜以喻勸諫無效，遂向十方祈願；大梵天王那羅陀化身苦行者降臨，與王賭五五百錢對來世一千，並開示無信者將墮諸地獄之慘狀，王戰慄懺悔，受五戒，轉行布施。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: After converting Uruvela-Kassapa the Buddha came to Latthivana, where the king of Magadha's followers disputed whether Kassapa was the teacher or the disciple; the elder laid his head on the Buddha's feet and rose seven times into the air. It is no marvel now, said the Master; of old, when I was the Brahma named Narada, still subject to passion, I burst this man's bonds of error. In Mithila the righteous king Angati had one daughter, Ruja, of great merit, and three ministers. On a full-moon night he asked each what pleasure they would have: Alata would conquer, Sunama would feast, and Vijaya would hear the Law - and so the king drove to the deer-park to consult the naked ascetic Guna of the Kassapa family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mahanaradakassapa Jataka (no. 544) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Guna taught that there is no fruit, good or evil, in following the law; no other world - who has ever come back from thence? Seven indestructible aggregates, fire, earth, water, air, pleasure, pain and soul, pass through eighty-four great aeons to purity, and weapons pass harmlessly among them. Alata confirmed it from his memory as a butcher who prospered; the slave Bijaka, who fasted and hurt nothing yet was born a beggar, wept that virtue bore no fruit - and the king embraced destiny, bade his ministers judge the suits, and gave himself to pleasure. His daughter Ruja, who remembered seven former births - a smith's son corrupted by evil friends and burned in the Roruva hell, a castrated goat, a mutilated monkey, an ox, one neither man nor woman among the Vajjis, then a nymph of Nandana with seven happy births to come - pleaded all night in parables: as a merchant's overloaded ship sinks, so a man laden with sin little by little sinks into hell; as the balance swings when the weight is laid, so merit gathered little by little raises a man's fate. But parents' love is strong and the king kept his heresy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mahanaradakassapa Jataka (no. 544) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Ruja worshipped the ten directions, praying that some righteous power would come to her father's rescue; and Great Brahma Narada, the Bodhisatta of that age, scanning the world, came down in the garb of an ascetic, matted hair and golden needle, antelope hide starred with gold. Ask me, he said; and the king wagered: if there is another world, give me five hundred pieces here and I will give you a thousand there. Fools lend to the idle and the cruel, Narada answered, but to the virtuous and generous men invite the loan; and he numbered the hells - ravens and vultures devouring the torn body, the blind tumultuous dark between three worlds, arrows and flaming coals raining on the cruel, chariots driven over the fiery ground, razor mountains, the silk-cotton tree of iron thorns, the river Vetarani. Who would press such a wretch for his thousand pieces?
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mahanaradakassapa Jataka (no. 544) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king trembled like a tree being felled, took the sage for his refuge, was taught the path of purity and the chariot-of-the-body parable, gave up false doctrine, took the five precepts, and turned to almsgiving; and Narada praised Ruja before all and passed through the air to the Brahma world. The naked ascetic Guna was Sunakkhatta, Ananda was Ruja, Uruvela-Kassapa was the king, and the Bodhisatta was Great Brahma.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Mahanaradakassapa Jataka (no. 544) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

title.en: Vidhura Wagered at Dice (Vidhurapandita Jataka, no. 545)
title.zh: 維陀羅智臣本生（第五百四十五）

texts.period: Jataka no. 545, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by E. B. Cowell, 1907

region.en: Indapatta in the Kuru country; the Black Mountain and the Naga palace (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧國因陀羅波達城；黑山與龍宮（象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 6 (trans. E. B. Cowell, 1907)

summary.en: Queen Vimala of the Nagas feigns a craving for the heart of the sage Vidhura, counselor of the Kuru king; her daughter Irandati is promised to the yakkha Punnaka if he can win the sage at dice. Punnaka conquers with a stolen jewel and a magic steed, carries Vidhura hanging by the horse's tail to the Black Mountain, tries lion, elephant, serpent and precipice in vain, is shamed by the four duties of the good man, and - the sage having converted the Naga court - flies him home in triumph.
summary.zh: 龍后雲母假裝渴望「智臣維陀羅之心」，其女伊蘭達蒂答應嫁給夜叉朋那迦，條件是贏得智者；朋那迦以竊取的摩尼寶珠與神駒與好賭的健馱邏王擲骰獲勝，令維陀羅手執馬尾凌空飛至黑山，化獅、化象、化蛇、掀山、颶風皆不能使其動一毛；智臣以「善人四法」感化夜叉，又度化龍宮王后，功成返國。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: In Indapatta of the Kuru country served the minister Vidhurapandita, whose sweet discourses on the Law held a hundred kings as elephants are held by a lute. Once four fasters met in the royal park - Sakka down from heaven, the Naga king Varuna, the Supanna king, and Dhananjaya Koravya - each claiming his virtue best; Vidhura judged all four one, like spokes in one nave, and each gave him gifts. When Varuna went home without his jewel, his queen Vimala longed to hear the sage and feigned a sick woman's craving: I desire Vidhura's heart brought here without guile. Who will bring him? the king asked, and bade his daughter Irandati find a husband who could.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Vidhurapandita Jataka (no. 545) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Irandati sang on a flower-strewn Himalayan height for a husband able to grant all desires, and Punnaka, nephew of Vessavana Kuvera, riding a Sindh horse three leagues long, heard the voice pierce to his bones and claimed her. The Naga king set the bride-price: bring me the sage's heart won in fair fight. Punnaka stole the priceless jewel of the universal monarch from Mount Vepulla, showed the Kuru king his steed galloping the city wall and standing on his palm, dazzled him with the jewel that holds a created world in it, and challenged him to dice. The king's guardian goddess fled Punnaka's widened eyes; three throws fell against the king, and though he cried that Vidhura was his refuge and defence, like his life, Vidhura himself settled it: I am the king's slave from my birth; he may give me by right. Then he begged three days to exhort his thousand sons - the last sight of him - and taught them at length how a man dwells honourably in a king's court.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Vidhurapandita Jataka (no. 545) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Take the tail of my steed, said Punnaka; this is thy last sight of the living world. Of whom shall I be afraid, who have done evil to no one? cried Vidhura, and seized the tail as the horse bounded skyward to the Black Mountain, sixty leagues high. Punnaka became a frightful demon, a lion, a furious elephant, a trough-sized serpent coiling over his head; he raised a mighty wind, shook the mountain like a wild date palm, roared from its belly - and not a hair of the sage stirred. Whirling him head-downwards over the void, the yakkha confessed his errand: the Naga maiden Irandati is to be won with the sage's heart. Hold me up, said Vidhura, and I will declare to thee all the laws of the good man: follow the path of hospitality already traversed; burn not the wet hand - betray not the host who fed thee; break not the bough of the tree that shelters thee; trust not the wanton woman. Punnaka counted himself traitor in every clause: let all that concerns the Naga race perish - I have had enough of the Naga maiden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Vidhurapandita Jataka (no. 545) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Send me not home but carry me to the Naga dwelling, said the sage; it is my task now to soften the Naga king. Before Varuna he asked how such a palace was won - by my own virtuous deeds, said the Naga; I and my wife in the world of men were full of faith and bountiful. Then practise virtue still, said Vidhura, and sin not toward the snakes born here. To Vimala he gave the same answers, and she was satisfied; the heart of sages is their wisdom, declared the Naga king, and gave Irandati at once to Punnaka, who showered Vidhura with jewels and flew him home to Indapatta, setting him down amid the weeping court. Dhananjaya, who had dreamed of the wisdom-tree cut down and replanted, proclaimed a month of festival, freed every captive in the realm, and Vidhura taught on until his life was full and he was destined for heaven. The Naga king Varuna was Sariputta, the garula king Moggallana, Sakka was Anuruddha, Dhananjaya was Ananda, and the wise Vidhura was I myself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Vidhurapandita Jataka (no. 545) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

title.en: Vessantara, the Perfect Giver (Vessantara Jataka, no. 547)
title.zh: 須大拏太子本生（第五百四十七）

texts.period: Jataka no. 547, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by E. B. Cowell, 1907

region.en: Jetuttara, city of King Sivi, and Mount Vamka in the Himalaya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 屍毘國逝多頓羅城與雪山溫迦山（象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 6 (trans. E. B. Cowell, 1907)

summary.en: Born on a plea from heaven to be the world's perfect giver, Vessantara gives away the rain-elephant in a famine, is banished with wife Maddi and their two children to Mount Vamka, gives horses, chariot, and then his children to the brahmin Jujuka, and - when Sakka in disguise begs for Maddi - gives her too; his Act of Truth, Sakka's eight boons and his father's penitence restore everything, and a rain of jewels fills Jetuttara.
summary.zh: 帝釋應天界宿願送下「圓滿布施」的須大拏太子；因饑荒施捨祈雨寶象而遭放逐，攜妻美帝與一雙兒女流放溫迦山；繼施車馬，終將一對兒女施予老婆羅門鳩迦，乃至帝釋假扮婆羅門索其妻，亦欣然與之；後因諦誓之力、帝釋八願與祖父懺悔，一家團圓，重登王位，帝釋復降寶雨充盈都城。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Vessantara story is actively recited in Theravada festival contexts (Thailand, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia, Sri Lanka) and is retold freely; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Visiting his proud Sakya kinsmen, the Buddha rose into the air and performed the twofold miracle, and his father bowed to him a third time - on his birth, at the ploughing festival, now - till every kinsman followed; then a great cloud burst in a shower that wetted those who wished and left the rest dry. Not the first time, said the Buddha, has rain fallen on my kinsfolk. Long before, in Jetuttara, Phusati - a heaven-born queen who in the age of the Buddha Vipassi had prayed to bear a perfect giver, and dying in heaven had chosen ten boons of Sakka - bore such a son: born in the Vessa street, holding out his hand at birth to ask for something to give, named Vessantara, with the white elephant Paccaya dropped into the royal stables the same day. At eight, meditating on giving his own heart and eyes, he shook the earth; at sixteen he was crowned, married Maddi, and had Jali and Kanhajina.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Vessantara Jataka (no. 547) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Famine came on Kalinga, and its king sent eight brahmins for the rain-elephant. At the southern gate they cried, Victory to the noble Vessantara! - and from the elephant's back he gave the precious beast with all its jeweled trappings, while the earth quaked and the city rang. The people's wrath forced even King Sanjaya: banish him to Vamka hill, they cried. The king bought one night's grace, and Vessantara spent it in the gift of the Seven Hundreds - seven hundred elephants, horses, chariots, maidens, cows, slaves - then took the road with Maddi, who chose exile over widowhood: as Sita did for Rama, so I for my husband care. Four brahmins took the horses, a fifth the chariot, while gods in the shape of red deer drew it on; the fruit trees bowed their branches to the children; the gods shortened the sixty-league road to a day. Refusing his uncle's crown at the Ceta court, he came to the hermitage Vissakamma built by the foursquare lake, and there Maddi fetched the wild fruits while he minded the children, and they vowed not to approach each other unseasonably.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Vessantara Jataka (no. 547) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: In Dunnivittha of Kalinga the old brahmin Jujuka had a young wife whom the village women mocked at the river. Maddi's nightmare of a black man tearing out her heart is the omen, and Vessantara sends her out as usual. Give me your children! - the children fled to hide in the lake, then came out at their father's call and clung to his feet weeping. I give, and shrink not, said Vessantara, and poured the water of gift, praying that omniscience, dearer a thousandfold than his son, ripen from the deed. Jujuka bound the two with a creeper and drove them like calves, pricing them - a thousand gold pieces for Jali, a hundred-each ransom for Kanhajina - and the father, shut in his hut, trembled like the moon in Rahu's jaws, yet mastered his grief: to give and repent is not the way of the righteous. Maddi, held back by a lion, tiger and pard set upon her path by the gods, searched fifteen leagues of forest through the night, found the hermitage empty, and fell as dead at his feet. Raised and told, she rejoiced: I do rejoice - a greater gift than children cannot be.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Vessantara Jataka (no. 547) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Fearing a vile suitor might take Maddi, Sakka came at dawn as an old brahmin and begged for her. Weary am I, said Vessantara, yet I give, and shrink not; and the portents shook heaven again. Maddi said only: from maidenhood I was his wife, let him give, or sell, or kill - and Sakka praised her resolution, restored her at once, and offered eight boons, among them that his father recall him without penalty and that he be born no more on earth. Jujuka drove the children to Jetuttara, where their grandfather ransomed them; and Jujuka, feasting on his gains, ate himself to death. Sanjaya marched to Vamka; Vessantara feared the worst until Maddi knew their own banners, and the old king confessed: it was ill done of me to ruin the innocent. The royal family fainted together in a swoon, and Sakka sent the selective rain again. Consecrated again, Vessantara freed every captive, and Sakka rained jewels knee-deep over Jetuttara to supply his giving forever; then, fully wise, he passed to heaven. Devadatta was Jujuka, Suddhodana was Sanjaya, Mahamaya was Phusati, Rahula's mother was Maddi, Rahula was Jali, Anuruddha was Sakka, and King Vessantara was I myself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Vessantara Jataka (no. 547) (Cowell 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: The Jataka, vol. VI, no. 547 (Pali Text Society translation series, 1907), pp. 246-305; the Pali text with commentary is V. Fausboell, The Jataka together with its Commentary, vol. VI (1896). The story runs to roughly a thousand stanzas and is the only Jataka traditionally reckoned to include complete chapter divisions (khandas).

narrative.en:
The Vessantara Jataka is the longest, most elaborated and most celebrated of the 547 birth-stories of the Pali collection, and in Theravada Asia it functions almost as a separate scripture. The frame sets it at the Buddha's return to Kapilavatthu: his proud Sakya kinsmen refuse him obeisance until he rises into the air and performs the twofold miracle, his father Suddhodana bows for the third time in his life, and a marvellous cloud bursts in a selective shower that wets only those who wish to be wet. A rain like that, says the Buddha, once fell on my kinsfolk - and he tells the story of Vessantara, a story the tradition treats as the final and perfect rehearsal of the Bodhisatta's career as a giver.

The tale opens in heaven. Two princesses of the age of the Buddha Vipassi had offered him sandal-powder and a golden wreath: the elder prayed to become the mother of a Buddha (and became Queen Maya), the younger prayed for a son of incomparable generosity. Passing through the divine worlds, she stood at last before Sakka with her merit spent, and from him she chose ten boons - dark fawn's eyes, undimmed beauty, and above all a son glorious, bounteous and ungrudging. Sakka brought the Bodhisatta down from the Thirty-three to fill that boon, with sixty thousand gods born as his retinue. The queen's pregnancy announced itself in six alms-halls and six hundred thousand pieces given daily; the boy was born in the Vessa street of Jetuttara, and at the moment of birth held out his hand and asked for something to give - three times in his long history had a Bodhisatta spoken at birth. A flying elephant left its white calf, Paccaya, in the royal stables the same day. At eight years old, lying on his couch, he resolved to give his heart, his flesh, his eyes; the earth of forty thousand quadrillions of leagues thundered, Sineru bowed, and Sakka clapped his arms.

Crowned at sixteen and married to his cousin Maddi, he gave on as before - until famine struck Kalinga, and eight brahmins came begging the white rain-elephant. Mounted on Paccaya's back, Vessantara gave the state elephant with every jeweled trapping. The earth quaked; the city rang with fury; the throne itself shook. The Sivi folk demanded that the giver be banished to Vamka hill, and King Sanjaya, powerless before the crowd, bought a single night's grace. His son spent it in the gift of the Seven Hundreds - seven hundred elephants, horses, chariots, maidens, cows, men- and women-slaves - and when Maddi, told of the sentence, chose exile over a widow's life ('as Sita did for Rama, so I care for my husband'), the family drove out in a chariot whose horses were given to four brahmins, whose chariot was given to a fifth, and whose pole, once the gods came disguised as red deer to draw it, was pulled along roads the gods shortened until a sixty-league journey took a day. His uncle offered him the Ceta crown; he refused it, and in the Himalaya the divine craftsman Vissakamma built the hermit family two houses by the foursquare lake. Maddi gathered the wild fruits and Vessantara minded the children, and to guard his chastity in the wilderness they vowed never to approach each other unseasonably.

The crisis arrives through an old man's shame. Jujuka, a brahmin of Dunnivittha in Kalinga, has married a young wife whom the village women taunt at the river: fetch slaves to serve you, or begone. Led by the gods, he finds the hermitage. Maddi's nightmare - a black man tearing out her heart - is the omen; Vessantara reads it rightly and sends her out as usual. The children flee to hide in the lake, but at their father's call they come out and cling to his feet, weeping, asking whether he will sell them while their mother is away. I give, and shrink not, he says, and pours the water of gift, praying that omniscience - dearer a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold than his son - may ripen from the deed, while the earth resounds to Brahma's heaven. Jujuka binds the two children wrist to wrist with a bit of creeper and drives them away beating them, pricing them aloud as a man prices cattle - a thousand gold pieces for the boy, a hundred of everything for the girl - and the king, shut in his hut, trembles like the moon in Rahu's jaws and thinks of running the man down and killing him; then he remembers that to give and then to repent is not the way of the righteous, and sits still, weeping tears that feel like drops of blood.

Maddi, meanwhile, is held back by a lion, a tiger and a pard that the gods have set on her path to keep her from the road; she reaches home after dark, finds the hermitage empty, and searches the forest - fifteen leagues of ground covered in one night - before she falls senseless at her husband's feet. He revives her with water, tells her plainly, and she answers with the story's hardest sentence of praise: I do rejoice; a greater gift than children cannot be. Sakka, fearing that some vile suitor may now come for Maddi and leave the giver destitute, arrives at dawn disguised as an old brahmin and begs for her. Weary am I, Vessantara says, yet in my own despite I give, and shrink not - and the portents thunder again. Maddi looks on in silence and speaks like a lion: from maidenhood I was his wife; let him give me, or sell me, or kill me. Sakka praises them both, gives her back on the spot, and offers eight boons, among them that his father recall him without penalty, that he never condemn a man to death, that Jali live long, and that Vessantara be born no more on earth.

The restoration is as symmetric as the fall. Jujuka drives the children to Jetuttara, where their grandfather recognizes them by their likeness, ransoms them at exactly the price their father fixed - and Jujuka, gorged with the payment and his new seven-storeyed palace, eats himself to death. Sanjaya marches fourteen thousand elephants, horses and chariots to Vamka; Vessantara hears the host and fears his father has been slain and he hunted next, until Maddi recognizes their own banners. The old king confesses: it was ill done of me to ruin the innocent. King, queen, son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren faint together in one embrace, and Sakka sends down the selective rain a second time. Re-consecrated, Vessantara frees every captive in the realm, and Sakka's rain of seven kinds of jewels - waist-deep at the palace, knee-deep in the streets - supplies his giving for the rest of his life; he dies fully wise and passes to heaven. The Jataka closes with its roll of identities: Devadatta was Jujuka, Rahula was Jali, Rahula's mother was Maddi - and King Vessantara was the Buddha himself.

Down the centuries the story has been the most-performed text of the Theravada world. In Thailand and Laos it is the kernel of the Bun Phra Wet (merit-making of the Prince Wet) festival, recited through a day and a night by specialist chanters whose different voices carry the different roles; villagers sponsor the recitation for rain, merit and the transfer of merit to the dead, and the final chapter, the gift of Maddi, is customarily read at dawn. In Burma, Cambodia, Sri Lanka and among Tai communities of Yunnan and Vietnam the story circulates in local verse and painted scroll, and its last life-before-awakening status makes it the paradigm of the parami of dana. It is also, within the tradition itself, the standing provocation of an ethical argument: preachers from the commentaries to modern village sermons have had to explain how a father may give away his children and a husband his wife, and the text itself stages the debate in Maddi's swoon, her consent, the king's blame of his son, and the children's reproach - a debate about where the perfection of giving ends and ordinary human duty begins, which the canon resolves by joy rather than by casuistry.

functions: Charter of the perfection of giving (dana-paramita): the tradition treats Vessantara as the Bodhisatta's final and fullest rehearsal of generosity before awakening, the model against which every act of dana is measured.

Festival and ritual engine: as the text of the Bun Phra Wet (Bun Bang Fai-adjacent) recitations of Thailand, Laos and neighbouring Tai regions, the Vessantara recital is sponsored for rain, harvest, merit-transfer to the dead, and communal merit-making; in many villages the recitation is a major annual obligation.

Moral provocation and teaching device: the gift of the children and of Maddi is the tradition's classic dilemma on the limits of giving versus family duty, used in sermons to teach both the supremacy of the parami and the joy (not merely endurance) expected of the giver.

Royal and political ideology: kings and patrons across Theravada Asia have sponsored Vessantara recitations and Vessantara-themed art to identify their rule with the cakkavatti ideal of unfailing, ungrudging generosity; the story's closing 'king and queen restored' scene legitimates restoration and amnesty.

variants.description: Tibetan Kanjur cycle 'Prince Vishvantara' (Tib. gZungs-bla'i sras / Vishvantara), translated from Sanskrit sources rather than the Pali: the prince is exiled for giving the rain-elephant, gives away his children to an old brahmin and then his wife Madri, and is restored. The corpus already carries three Tibetan records of this cycle (tibetan-visvantara-exile, tibetan-visvantara-children, tibetan-visvantara-restored) keyed to the character id visvantara, which is the Sanskrit form of the same figure as Pali Vessantara; see also 'tibetan-visvantara-children' for the parallel gift of the two children.
variants.name: tibetan-visvantara-exile
variants.summary: Related telling of the Vessantara story.

variants.description: Sanskrit parallels outside the Kanjur: the Sibi cycle (the king who gives his eyes, Avadanasataka and Suvarnabhasottama-sutra) and the Mahavastu's Jataka-material on giving share the test-by-disguised-god, the Act of Truth, and the restoration-by-boon structure of this story; the Chinese King of Khotanese and Khotanese 'Sudana' (Sudatta/Vessantara) versions and the Jataka-mala's Vishvantara chapter (Arya Sura, ch. 9) are the closest literary relatives in the Sanskrit tradition.
variants.name: none
variants.summary: Related telling of the Vessantara story.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Vessantara Jataka is actively recited and festival-performed across the Theravada world (Thailand, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia, Sri Lanka and Tai communities elsewhere); it is a living devotional text, not a museum artefact. Retell it respectfully: the gift of the children and of Maddi should be presented as the tradition's own debated ethical extreme (with Maddi's consent and the text's inner criticism included), never as a comic or 'barbaric' curiosity; avoid illustrations that mock monastic or royal figures; and note that in many Tai villages the recitation is still a solemn rain-making and merit-transfer rite.
